sections.h2: Why did Central become its own city, and what does that mean for sellers?
sections.html:
Central became a city on April 23, 2005, after residents voted to incorporate, and a house here is now governed by the City of Central rather than the Baton Rouge city-parish. The move came despite opposition from the parish.

According to Wikipedia, businessman Russell Starns led the effort, which grew out of a wish to have a school system separate from East Baton Rouge Parish's. The Legislature allowed a separate system only after the city incorporated. Central had about 25,000 residents at the time, and residents are zoned to the Central Community School System.

For a seller, the practical point is that permits, planning and floodplain questions go to Central City Hall at 11530 Sullivan Road, phone 225.262.5000. Recording of the deed, however, still happens at the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court because Central sits inside that parish.

sections.h2: Where is Central, and what is the land like?
sections.html:
Central is in the east-central part of East Baton Rouge Parish, between the Comite River on its west border and the Amite River, which forms the line with Livingston Parish. The two rivers meet near the city's southern edge.

The Census Bureau lists 62.26 square miles of land, which makes Central far larger in area than its population suggests. Louisiana Highway 408 runs through the center and leads about 7 miles west to Interstate 110 in north Baton Rouge. Louisiana Highway 37 crosses the eastern side. Downtown Baton Rouge is about 13 miles southwest.

With two rivers on its borders, where a house stands relative to the Comite and Amite is a fair first question when reviewing its flood history.

Source: Wikipedia: Central, Louisiana.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about Central homes?
sections.html:
Central is overwhelmingly a city of owner-occupied houses, with 88.8 percent of housing units owner-occupied for 2020 to 2024. The median value of those homes is $288,700, higher than in Baton Rouge itself.

The population was 29,565 in the 2020 census and 30,313 in the Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate. A market that is mostly owner-occupied means most sellers here are homeowners rather than landlords, and the usual reasons to sell quickly are a move, an inheritance, a divorce or repairs the owner cannot fund.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts for Central.

sections.h2: How did the 2016 flood affect Central?
sections.html:
Central was one of the hardest-hit parts of East Baton Rouge Parish in August 2016. WAFB reported significant flooding, and Mayor Jr. Shelton said the number of Central residents affected was 25,000.

The Army Corps of Engineers says the August 2016 flood far exceeded the flood of record in the Comite River basin, with about 109,000 homes flooded across Louisiana and 79,000 of them in East Baton Rouge and Livingston Parishes. The Comite River Diversion is the project meant to reduce headwater flooding on this side of the parish. It involves a 12-mile channel, 23 contracts and, as of the Corps' page, six projects under construction after all contracts were awarded by the end of fiscal year 2025.

Because of that history, a buyer in Central is likely to ask:

  • Did this house take water in 2016, and how deep?
  • Was it gutted and rebuilt with permits?
  • Is there an elevation certificate on file?
  • Is the property in a regulatory floodway or a repetitive loss area?

Sources: Army Corps Comite River Diversion, Wikipedia: Central, Louisiana.

sections.h2: What can Central's floodzone determination tell a seller?
sections.html:
The City of Central lets owners request a formal floodzone determination, and the result covers much more than a zone letter. It can include the base flood elevation, a Community-Defined Flood Elevation, the FIRM panel number and effective date, and whether the property is in a regulatory floodway or a conveyance zone.

It can also state whether the property is in a repetitive loss area and the 2016 flood depth at the property. For a seller, that last item answers the most common buyer question with an official number instead of a rumor.

  • The city keeps elevation certificates on file for structures completed after 2008 and publishes a list of those properties.
  • An owner whose elevation certificate shows the structure is above the flood level may qualify to seek removal from the floodplain through a Letter of Map Change.
  • Central takes part in the Community Rating System, which can lower flood insurance premiums for policy holders.

Ordering the determination before you list takes one question off the table and gives a buyer's lender a document to work from.

Source: City of Central floodplain management.

sections.h2: What permits does Central require, and when do repairs need one?
sections.html:
Central requires permits for most work beyond cosmetic touch-ups, including remodels, additions, roofing, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work, fences, generators and demolitions. Accessory buildings over 200 square feet and portable structures over 120 square feet also need a permit.

A separate disturbance permit is required before using mechanized equipment to disturb land, remove trees by machine, haul in more than 12 cubic yards of soil, sand or fill, or demolish a structure with heavy equipment. The floodplain manager may approve up to 12 inches of fill without a geotechnical report. Anything deeper needs engineered lifts, a geotechnical report and a topography plan by a licensed civil engineer, and it must not harm drainage on neighboring land.

The Permit Desk can be reached at 225.262.5000, extension 1. The city has also dropped its separate trade contractor license as a prerequisite for permit approval.

This matters at sale time. If you raised a yard, added a carport or replaced a roof without a permit, a buyer's inspector or lender may flag it. Unpermitted work is easier to fix before an offer than after.

Source: City of Central permits and inspections.

sections.h2: How does a sale close in Central, and which route fits?
sections.html:
A Central sale closes the same way as any Louisiana sale. The Civil Code requires a sale of an immovable to be made by authentic act or by act under private signature, so you sign before a notary and the act is recorded with the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court.

That clerk's Recording Department can be reached at (225) 389-3985, and fees are due when a document is recorded. The Louisiana Real Estate Commission's 2026 mandatory forms, including the Property Disclosure, took effect on January 1, 2026.

  • Listing: Works for a repaired, dry house where you can wait for financing and an appraisal.
  • Selling as-is for cash: Fits a house with flood repairs, deferred work or a deadline.
  • Selling by owner: Saves the agent's role but leaves the paperwork and buyer screening with you.

Act 807 of the 2026 session added rules for wholesaling residential real estate, and the Commission now publishes a mandatory cancellation notice. Ask any buyer whether they plan to assign your contract.

Sources: EBR Clerk of Court, LREC forms notice, LREC Act 807 notice.

faqs.q: Is Central part of Baton Rouge?
faqs.a: No. Central is its own city, incorporated on April 23, 2005, though it lies in East Baton Rouge Parish and belongs to the Baton Rouge metro area. It has its own city government and its own school system.

faqs.q: Which school system serves Central, LA?
faqs.a: The Central Community School System. Residents are zoned to it rather than to the East Baton Rouge Parish school system, because the Legislature allowed a separate system once the city incorporated.

faqs.q: How can I find out how deep the 2016 flood was at my Central house?
faqs.a: Request a floodzone determination from the City of Central. Its determinations can include the 2016 flood depth at the property, the base flood elevation, the FIRM panel and whether the property is in a floodway or repetitive loss area.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed for a house in Central?
faqs.a: At the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court, Recording Department, phone (225) 389-3985. Fees are due when the document is recorded.

faqs.q: What share of Central homes are owner-occupied?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau lists 88.8 percent of housing units as owner-occupied for 2020 to 2024, with a median owner-occupied home value of $288,700. These are citywide figures, not a value for any one house.
